say.2.5 to 3%: two and a half to three percent
say.580 °C: five hundred and eighty degrees Celsius

scenes.narration: Every bottle starts its life *upside down*.
Seconds after it's made, it goes straight *back into the heat*.
A big machine can make nearly *eight bottles a second*.
scenes.label: 470 bottles a minute

scenes.narration: To see why, follow one bottle, from a pile of sand to your hand.

scenes.title: The Recipe
scenes.narration: It begins as sand.
About *70%* of the mix.
But pure silica melts at about *1,700 °C*, far too hot and too thick to work.
scenes.label: Silica melts near 1,700 °C

scenes.narration: So soda ash goes in, and it drags the melting point *dramatically down*.
There's a catch. Soda makes glass *dissolve in water*.
A bottle that dissolves is useless, so limestone goes in to lock the glass.
Last comes *cullet*: crushed old glass that cuts the furnace's energy bill.
Every 10% of it saves about *2.5 to 3%* of the energy.
scenes.label: 2.5 to 3% less energy

scenes.narration: Machines weigh every part, because the recipe has to be exact.

scenes.title: The Furnace
scenes.narration: Into the furnace.
It runs around the clock, all year, for *eight to ten years* at a stretch.
Inside, the glass reaches about *1,600 °C*, hot enough to glow almost white.
scenes.label: About 1,600 °C

scenes.narration: As the mix melts, it fills with tiny *gas bubbles*.
Leave them in, and they end up in your bottle.
So chemicals like sodium sulfate release gas that helps clear them out.
The clean glass slides into a long channel called the *forehearth*.
There it cools to about *1,100 °C*, stiff enough to hold a shape.
scenes.label: About 1,100 °C

scenes.title: The Gob
scenes.narration: Now the stream gets cut.
Steel shears slice it into measured lumps called *gobs*.
Each gob is exactly one bottle, so its weight has to be right.
Gravity alone carries it down through chutes toward the machine.
That machine has up to *twenty sections*, each making up to four bottles at once.
scenes.label: Up to 20 sections

scenes.title: The Flip
scenes.narration: This is where it gets strange.
The first mould is *upside down*. The neck gets made first, at the bottom.
A metal plunger *rises* into the soft glass.
It presses the neck and a hollow starter shape called a *parison*.
That plunger has to be heatproof, and thin enough to fit a narrow neck.
Pressing keeps the walls even, which is how bottles got so light.
Now the flip.
An arm grips the neck and swings the parison over, a full *180°*.
It lands right way up, inside a second mould.
The halves close, and *compressed air* blows in through the neck.
The soft glass swells out until it hits the metal walls and takes their shape.
The mould opens, and there it is: a bottle, made in *seconds*.

scenes.title: Back Into The Heat
scenes.narration: It looks finished. It isn't.
The glass has just dropped from about 1,100 to *600 °C* in around *ten seconds*.
scenes.label: About 10 seconds

scenes.narration: The outside cooled fast. The inside stayed hotter. That fight is now locked in as *stress*.
Left like this, the bottle is weak, and it can crack all by itself.
First it passes under a hood of *tin vapour*, which leaves a very thin film.
That film gives the next coating something to grip.
Then it goes straight back into the heat, into a long oven called a *lehr*.
The lehr heats it to about *580 °C*, and the stress starts to let go.
scenes.label: About 580 °C

scenes.narration: Then it cools slowly, over *20 to 60 minutes*, depending on how thick the glass is.
scenes.label: 20 to 60 minutes

scenes.narration: That slow walk through the heat is what keeps it from breaking.

scenes.title: The Test
scenes.narration: Now it has to pass.
A waxy coating goes on, so bottles slide past each other without scratching.
Then every single bottle is inspected.
Machines hunt for tiny cracks called *checks*, plus stones, bubbles and thin walls.
Each bottle carries a mould number, so a flaw can be traced to the exact mould.
Anything that fails is rejected. The rest are packed and shipped.
So this is the bottle in your hand.
Made upside down, flipped over and blown into shape, all in seconds.
Then sent back through the heat, just so it wouldn't break.
Clean glass can be melted into new bottles again and again.
So when this one comes back as cullet, it starts all over.
Upside down.
